newsitem.title: FRANCE: Historians, archivists seek Holocaust guide.
newsitem.headline: Historians, archivists seek Holocaust guide.

text.p: More than 50 years after World War Two, historians are finding new insights into the Nazi Holocaust thanks to the opening of archives formerly shut off in the communist East.

Researchers and archivists from across Europe and the United States began a three-day congress on Sunday night to pool widely scattered sources of information on the extermination of six million European Jews.

The convention, hosted by the U.N. cultural agency UNESCO and organised by France's Contemporary Jewish Document Centre with European Union funding, is aimed partly at harnessing new archives in Eastern Europe that had been closed to Holocaust scholars until the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

"To find out why certain things happened, we have to go to hundreds of archives. I don't want to go to 100 or 200 or 300 places to find what I need," said U.S. historian Raul Hilberg, a leading authority on the Holocaust.
"We must discuss the re-concentration of these sources," he said.

One aim of the conference is to get researchers from some 25 European countries, the United States and Israel to work together on a guide to Holocaust archives, making it easier for future historians to find key sources.
Hilberg cited as an example his efforts to discover why Jews from the Netherlands were deported to the Sobibor death camp in Poland.

He eventually found the answer in Minsk, capital of the former Soviet state of Belarus, where a wealth of railway records on the organisation of special deportation trains had lain unexplored since the Red Army carried them off in 1945.

Even in Western democracies such as France, some archives are still closed or only opening slowly. French historian Andre Kaspi said soon-to-be-published records from the 1940-44 period show French diplomats reported in detail to the collaborationist Vichy government on the deportation and extermination of central European Jews, but their testimony was ignored.
Jean Kahn, president of the European Centre for Research and Action against Racism and Antisemitism, a co-organiser, said the ownership of archives can itself be politically sensitive.

President Jacques Chirac recently upset some historians by agreeing to deposit World War Two French police files on the Jews, discovered by Nazi hunter Serge Klarsfeld, at the Jewish document centre under the authority of the National Archives.
Three leading French historians complained in a letter to the newspaper Le Monde that these were French state archives, not Jewish documents, and should not be given to one community.

The Paris conference aims to promote serious research by the younger generation of historians and discourage what French historian Andre Kaspi called "Americanisation...sensationalism and emotionalism".

Kaspi cited as an example of the latter a controversial recent book by Harvard University historian Daniel Goldhagen which argues the German people were willing accomplices of Hitler due to a deep-seated tradition of German antisemitism.

Tel Aviv University professor Saul Friedlander joined Kaspi in disputing Goldhagen's thesis, saying that while recent research shows many ordinary Germans had indeed become willing executioners when given a choice, this could not be explained by any specific German strain of antisemitism.
"I do not see that there was agitation in the general population calling for the expulsion, much less the extermination of the Jews in the 1920s or 1930s," he said.

Among the many subjects the historians said remained to be explored are the history of local Jewish communities, the behaviour of Jews faced with extermination -- long taboo -- and the Germans' ethnic hierarchy among occupied peoples.
French Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy told the opening session his government strongly supported Holocaust research as a way of combating extreme-right revisionist and negationist propaganda.
